title: AI Super-Sleuth Finds 100+ Hidden Planets, Including a World That Orbits in Just One Day!
summary: Have you ever tried to find a tiny firefly next to a giant spotlight? That's what planet hunters do! They look for tiny dips in starlight when a planet passes in front of its star. Now, a clever AI named RAVEN has found over 100 hidden planets in data from NASA's TESS telescope. TESS watched more than 2.2 million stars for four years. RAVEN, built by scientists at the University of Warwick, is like a super-smart detective. It can tell if a dip in light is really a planet or just a trick, like two stars crossing. The AI found 118 new planets and over 2,000 possible ones. Some are really extreme! There are planets that zoom around their star in less than a day. Others are in the "Neptunian desert"—a place where scientists thought planets couldn't exist. The team also found systems with multiple planets packed close together. Dr. Marina Lafarga Magro, who led the study, said RAVEN helps find the best planets to study later. The AI was trained on hundreds of thousands of fake planets and fake signals. This helps it spot real planets with amazing accuracy. The scientists also learned how common close-in planets are. About 9-10% of Sun-like stars have a planet orbiting very close. That's a much more precise number than before. Dr. David Armstrong said RAVEN doesn't just list planets—it gives a reliable map of what kinds of planets are out there. The team shared their tools so other scientists can explore the data too. Who knows what other weird worlds are waiting to be found?
why_it_matters: Discovering new planets helps us learn if Earth‑like worlds are common, which could inspire your future studies in science or even a career searching for life beyond our solar system.

background_read: NASA's TESS (Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite) was launched in 2018 and has discovered thousands of planet candidates by watching the brightness of over 200,000 nearby stars.
The first exoplanet around a Sun‑like star was found in 1995, and since then astronomers have confirmed over 5,500 exoplanets.
The 'Neptunian desert' is a real puzzle—a shortage of Neptune‑sized worlds in orbits very close to their stars that scientists are still trying to explain.
Article_Structure: WHO: Dr. Marina Lafarga Magro and her team at the University of Warwick.
WHAT: The AI RAVEN analyzed TESS data and found 118 new planets plus over 2,000 possible ones.
WHERE: In space, using data from NASA's TESS telescope, which watches the entire sky.
WHY: To build a reliable map of what kinds of planets exist and find the best ones for further study.

perspectives.description: RAVEN acts like a super‑sleuth, saving us years of work by spotting real planets among thousands of fake or confusing signals.
Training RAVEN on hundreds of thousands of fake planets and signals made it extremely accurate, showing how AI can solve complex pattern problems in science.
Knowing that 9‑10% of Sun‑like stars have a close‑in planet gives us a much more precise and reliable picture of our galaxy.
